painting-archimede.title: Archimedes of Syracuse
painting-archimede.caption: c. 287 BC – 212 BC · Oil on canvas, Italian school
painting-archimede.imageAlt: Painted portrait of Archimedes, a bearded old man drawing shapes with a compass.
painting-archimede.body: The scholar from Syracuse draws circles in the sand. We owe him the principle of the buoyant force, the upward push of a fluid on an object placed in it, and the cry “Eureka!” that the museum loves to recall.

painting-galilee.title: Galileo Galilei
painting-galilee.caption: 1564 – 1642 · Oil on canvas, Florentine school
painting-galilee.imageAlt: Painted portrait of Galileo holding a telescope, with a celestial globe beside him.
painting-galilee.body: Telescope in hand, Galileo looks at the visitor. He showed that without friction, all objects fall in the same way, and that an object moving in a straight line at a constant speed needs no force to keep going.

painting-newton.title: Isaac Newton
painting-newton.caption: 1643 – 1727 · Oil on canvas, English school
painting-newton.imageAlt: Painted portrait of Newton holding a prism that splits a ray of light.
painting-newton.body: A prism, a ray, seven colours. Newton wrote the three laws of motion and the law of gravity, but he also showed that white light is a mix of colours.

painting-curie.title: Marie Curie
painting-curie.caption: 1867 – 1934 · Oil on canvas, French school
painting-curie.imageAlt: Painted portrait of Marie Curie in her laboratory, near glowing glass vials.
painting-curie.body: Two Nobel Prizes, first in physics, then in chemistry. The glowing vials next to her remind us of radium, which was isolated in a shed on rue Lhomond after tonnes of ore were processed by hand.

poster.title: Physics: the laws of the world
poster.caption: Exhibition poster · Lithograph, 1926
poster.imageAlt: Art Deco poster: a stylised pendulum, atom orbits and a prism splitting light.
poster.body: A pendulum, an atom and a prism. The poster announces the museum's permanent exhibition. Nothing is hidden in it, but it is beautiful.

plaque-rules.title: Curator's note
plaque-rules.caption: Engraved plaque, near the office door
plaque-rules.body: “The office padlock opens in order of time: from the oldest to the most recent. The labels next to the paintings will tell you who lived first. Every frame has a digit on the back.”

bust-archimede.title: Bust of Archimedes
bust-archimede.caption: Carrara marble, 19th-century copy
bust-archimede.body: Under the base, a note in pencil: “The paintings do not lie, look behind them.” Someone has searched here before you.

vitrine-armillary.title: Armillary sphere
vitrine-armillary.caption: Brass and mahogany, Paris workshop, c. 1780
vitrine-armillary.body: The marked rings show the equator, the ecliptic and the tropics. People used it to find the position of the stars long before pocket telescopes.

vitrine-telescope.title: Astronomical telescope
vitrine-telescope.caption: Brass and leather on a tripod, c. 1850
vitrine-telescope.body: A telescope like Galileo's does not magnify much, but it can already show the moons of Jupiter. Museum visitors used this one until 1962.

desk-note.title: Curator's desk
desk-note.caption: Oak, green leather, dry inkwell
desk-note.body: Under the desk pad, a note in purple ink: “What the eye cannot see, black light reveals. Look at the wall.” The drawer, though, is empty.

chalkboard.title: Curator's blackboard
chalkboard.caption: Formulas from the syllabus, white chalk
chalkboard.imageAlt: Blackboard covered with physics formulas: F = m·a, p = F/S, E = mc², Q = m·c·ΔT, U = R·I.
chalkboard.body: The formulas used by the museum's stations. Useful to check a formula before you answer, or to find the one for potential energy.

uv-wall.title: Revealed message
uv-wall.caption: Invisible ink, only readable under UV light
uv-wall.body: “The safe opens with the potential energy due to gravity, in joules, of a {mass} kg mass placed at a height of {height} m. Use g = 10 m/s². Three digits, nothing more.”

uv-lamp.name: UV lamp
uv-lamp.description: Reveals invisible ink. Found in the guard's drawer.

fuse.name: Main fuse
fuse.description: The fuse for the gallery's fuse box.

case-key.name: Display case key
case-key.description: Opens the display case at Joule's Track.

announcement.title: An evening at the museum
announcement.body: Tonight, the Physics Museum is hosting an escape game. Those who get out will meet Albert Einstein, who will be there as a hologram. Each player's time and mistakes will be counted until they get out.

queue.title: Alone, but ready
queue.body: Your friends said no: a physics escape game is not their thing. You spent the whole night revising. At the entrance, the queue is long. The guard sneers: “Alone? Good luck. Lots of people give up.”

doors.title: Six seals to get out
doors.body: The gallery doors close behind you. Each station you solve gives you a seal, and the Hologram Room needs six. Search, read, look around: not everything is physics. The timer starts now.

hologram.greeting: Ah, there you are. Did you come alone? Few people make it to the end, and even fewer do it without a team.
hologram.praise: I watched you play. You answered, but you also searched, read, and dared to make mistakes. That's exactly how physics moves forward.
hologram.farewell: Imagination is more important than knowledge. Tonight, you showed that you have both. Now, let's see your score.
